### According to Kew Bulletin under the synonym Vesalea mexicana var. grandifolia

Landrein, S., Farjon, A. (2020). A monograph of Caprifoliaceae: Linnaeeae. Kew Bulletin 75: 1 doi:10.1007/s12225-018-9762-5

Type
    Mexico, Queretaro, Municipio, de Jalpan, Cerro Grande, 13 June 1991, B. Servin 1101 (holotype CAS!, isotype MEXU!).
Morphology General Habit
    Prostrate, rarely erect shrubs
Morphology Leaves
    Leaves coriaceous with a bullate adaxial surface and crenate margin
Morphology Branches
    Branchlets and leaves abaxial mid-veins densely hispid with hairs to 0.6 mm long
Morphology Reproductive morphology Flowers Corolla
    Corolla tube abruptly expanding into the throat.
Distribution
    Mexico. In the northeast of Queretaro and southwest of San Luis Potosí, V. mexicana var. grandifolia is extremely localised but also abundant, only four populations are known.
Ecology
    Outcrops of calcareous sedimentary rock with Agave dasylirioides and inside Pinus forest with Aphananthe, Arbutus, Cercocarpus, Cupressus, Quercus and Rhus; 2,100 – 2,650 m.
Conservation
    Vulnerable (VU). Vesalea mexicana var. grandifolia has been collected seven times from four different known localities; it was last collected in 2013. The Area of Occupancy is 6 km2 (2 km square grid) and the Extent of Occurrence is 12 km2. The population is very restricted but also very abundant with possibly more than 5,000 individuals in total. Three localities are within the Sierra Gorda Biosphere Reserve and one is located within an ecotourist reserve (La Trinidad). The latter reserve is well maintained but the Sierra Gorda Reserve allows local uses, such as plant and animal collecting and wood harvesting. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Note
    A feature of the population in the Sierra de San Miguelito are the galls present on most shrubs. The larvae of the causal agent seem to feed on and transform the floral buds and could have an effect on the fertility rate. It is possible that this gall is specific to V. coriacea as it has not been seen on other Vesalea species. Coriacea is a Latin adjective meaning leathery, referring to the texture of the leaves. Vesalea mexicana, V. subcoriacea and V. floribunda may also have coriaceous leaves.
